newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: ANZ STAFF VOTE TO STRIKE
Branches of the ANZ bank in New South Wales and Western Australia are expected to be severely disrupted tomorrow, when staff strike action.
In Western Australia, members of the Finance Sector Union set a deadline of yesterday afternoon for the ANZ to respond to their concerns, including voluntary redundancy and redeployment options.
Union Industrial Officer, Leon Carter, says the bank failed to address the issues, and members voted in favour of a 24-hour strike.
The strike is likely to affect all ANZ branches in WA, as well as Town and Country and Esanda Finance, which are owned by the ANZ.
There's likely to be similar action in Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania next Wednesday.
ANSETT KEEN FOR ASIAN EXPANSION
Ansett will today pitch for greater prominence on air routes between Australia and Hong Kong.

Officials from Ansett, Qantas and Cathay Pacific will attend a summit between the Australian and Hong Kong Governments today. They'll discuss the potential for an expansion of air capacity between the two countries.
Ansett currently runs five direct services from Sydney to Hong Kong, but is keen to expand, saying it's performed well internationally.
It says extra services to Hong Kong would help in its aim to consolidate its presence in the south east Asian market.
EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK STILL IN QUESTION
ACTU President Jennie George says the union movement will pursue a general statement of principles from the Industrial Relations Commission to end gender-based wage discrimination.
The ACTU has reached agreement outside the commission with Sydney manufacturer Utilux, delivering minor pay rises for women process workers.
It's now settled claims with the three companies it identified as potential vehicles to ensure equal pay for work of equal standing.
Ms George says Democrat amendments to the Workplace Relations bill will help ensure the recognition of equal pay for equal work.
She says further test cases will be pursued, particularly in the manufacturing sector.
SYDNEY'S FEMALE PRIEST DECISION TODAY
Women in the Anglican Church find out today if they can become priests in the Sydney diocese, following a three year moratorium on the issue.

While women are allowed to become priests in 14 dioceses across the country, in Sydney - the largest diocese in Australia - they're restricted to becoming deacons. At the recent Anglican Synod, the Movement for the Ordination of Women put forward an ordinance calling for women to be allowed as priests but not as heads of parishes, which was accepted by Church officials as less contentious.
JOURNALISTS BACK FREE SPEECH
The journalists' union says a High Court decision guaranteeing freedom of speech on political matters, which is to be opposed by the Federal Government, was a landmark judgement.
Attorney-General, Daryl Williams, says the court's ruling that there is an implied democratic right to freedom of speech on political matters in the Constitution went too far.
Mr Williams says the Commonwealth will argue against this in a High Court case next year, saying contentious political matters should be left to Parliament.
But Secretary of the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance, Chris Warren, says the court made the right decision.
Mr Warren says the case was probably the most important step forward for human rights and free speech in Australia.
FALLOUT FROM SALMONELLA OUTBREAK ON QANTAS FLIGHTS
Reports from Japan's health ministry that up to 350 Qantas passengers on flights between Japan and Cairns received food poisoning are being disputed by the airline.
The salmonella outbreak occurred earlier this month, and the ministry says 51 victims are still in hospital.
But Qantas says it won't speculate about how many people were poisoned until investigations are finalised.
A Qantas spokesman says it's received no more reports of people falling ill, and the airline's offered to pay the medical costs of those affected.
The airline will also look at compensating victims.
Federal tourism minister John Moore says he's concerned about the situation, but says he expects Qantas is doing its best to protect Australia's tourism industry.
MPS CALLED UPON TO PROTECT CHILDREN
Politicians are being urged to fulfil their obligations to children under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Chief Justice of the Family Court, Alastair Nicholson, says planned cuts to legal aid will have a direct impact on the welfare of children.
Speaking in Perth last night, Justice Nicholson said a lack of dialogue by federal or state governments on the funding issue provides the environment for a breach of the convention.
The Chief Justice says it's imperative that the training and funding of children's legal representatives be maintained.
He says problems are already beginning in WA and Victoria where Legal Aid Commissions are limiting child access to legal representatives.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
